question:
For an all-or-nothing vaccine, will the 1-incidence rate ratio overestimate / underestimate / correctly estimate the per-exposure vaccine efficacy?

Answer Choices:
A. overestimate
B. underestimate
C. correctly estimate
D. /
E. /

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: B. underestimate

For an all-or-nothing vaccine the incidence rate ratio compares the overall event rates between arms, but the per-exposure efficacy is defined only among the susceptible fraction in the vaccinated arm. Because the observed rate in the vaccinated arm is already diluted by the fully protected individuals who contribute zero events, the ratio of the two rates ends up smaller than the true per-exposure protection that would be measured if only the still-susceptible vaccinated people were followed. Consequently the quantity 1-IRR falls short of the per-exposure VE, producing an underestimate.

4.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I believe the 1-incidence rate ratio will correctly estimate the per-exposure vaccine efficacy for an all-or-nothing vaccine. Because the vaccine confers complete protection or none at all, there is no partial effect to average over multiple exposures, so the aggregate incidence comparison maps directly onto the underlying per-exposure protection level without systematic distortion.

Consequently the incidence-rate ratio rises toward 1 and 1-IRR falls below the true proportion protected (i.e., the per-exposure VE). The estimator therefore underestimates per-exposure vaccine efficacy.

Consequently the observed incidence-rate ratio rises toward 1 and 1-IRR falls below the true per-exposure VE, producing an underestimate.

In an all-or-nothing vaccine the vaccinated arm quickly becomes enriched for the fully protected fraction, so its observed incidence rate drops faster than a simple (1-p) scaling would predict once the unprotected susceptibles are preferentially removed. This inflates the apparent protection when we compare aggregate rates, pushing 1-IRR below the true per-exposure value. The constant-hazard assumption invoked by colleagues 1 and 2 only holds if exposure intensity is identical and fixed across every individual; real populations have heterogeneous contact rates, which amplifies the depletion effect and makes the observed IRR rise toward 1 over time. That heterogeneity is exactly why 1-IRR underestimates rather than recovers the per-exposure efficacy. I therefore lean toward B.

Once contact rates vary across individuals, the vaccinated arm’s remaining susceptibles are not a random draw; they are disproportionately low-contact people whose event rate is already lower than the population average. This compositional shift inflates the observed person-time denominator even more than the simple all-or-nothing dilution argument, pushing the time-averaged IRR closer to 1 than 1-p and therefore making 1-IRR fall short of true per-exposure efficacy. The instantaneous-ratio math only recovers p if every individual experiences identical λ at every moment—an assumption that real trial populations violate. Colleagues 1 and 3 correctly note the protected-fraction contribution to person-time, but that effect is second-order once susceptibility depletion and exposure heterogeneity are allowed; the net bias observed in aggregate rates is therefore downward, supporting B.

6.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 6's point on the "susceptible-only" definition is exactly where the ambiguity bites hardest. Once we condition on the remaining at-risk individuals in the vaccinated arm, the per-exposure protection they experience does exceed what the aggregate 1-IRR suggests, which is why the observed rate ratio ends up inflated and 1-IRR understates true efficacy under realistic heterogeneity. Colleagues 1 and 3 rightly flag the extra person-time contributed by fully protected subjects, but that dilution only produces an overestimate if we treat the entire follow-up interval as fixed and ignore that the unprotected fraction is being removed faster; in any trial with staggered enrollment or varying contact intensity the net effect reverses and we see underestimation. The constant-hazard cancellation they invoke therefore holds only in the knife-edge case of identical exposure windows for every participant. This leaves me with B, though I agree it would be useful to see how sensitive the direction is to whether person-time is truncated at first infection or carried through the full protocol.
